components.note: Durrett pp. 1, 3-4: sigma-field (with the sigma-field synonym), countable = finite or countably infinite, measurable space, algebra, generated sigma-field.
Durrett p. 1 (closure under intersections) and p. 3 (intersection over a nonempty, possibly uncountable index set; smallest sigma-field).
Durrett Ex. 1.1.6 (p. 4), the finite/cofinite algebra, rendered on N+ instead of Z with the same argument and the generated sigma-algebra added.
Durrett p. 1 measure and probability measure definitions; nonnegative extended sums defined.
Durrett Thm 1.1.1 (i)-(iv) (p. 2), including the finiteness premise for continuity from above.

components.gap: Durrett Ex. 1.1.2 (discrete probability spaces, 'the most general probability measure on this space') is covered with the grouping theorem. Not supplied: the example the source gives immediately after it (p. 3), the astragali, dice of ancient Egypt made from sheep ankle bones that rest on the top (4 points), bottom (3), flat narrow side (6) or rounded side (1), with the claim that there is no reason to think the four outcomes equally likely, so four separate probabilities p1, p3, p4, p6 are needed. This historical and empirical motivating case is not on the input route (its only rendering is in the uninserted w02c-p15-002 file).

components.note: Handbook example; geometric sums and continuity statements verified (even outcomes 1/3).
Worked boundary for the finiteness premise of Durrett Thm 1.1.1(iv); counting measure and the finitely additive non-extendable assignment verified.
Durrett p. 3: Borel sets as the sigma-field generated by the open sets of R^d.

components.gap: Durrett lists as generating classes for testing measurability the closed real rays and the open rational rays {(-infinity,x): x in Q} (Ex. 1.3.2, p. 15), and for R^d the open rectangles (a1,b1) x ... x (ad,bd) with real endpoints, 'or occasionally the larger collection of open sets' (Ex. 1.3.3, p. 15). The theorem states rational open rectangles and closed rational or real rays only. The open-rational-ray generator is stated nowhere on the input route (the annex shows only that open rays lie in the generated sigma-algebra), and the real-endpoint open rectangles are not stated as a generating class (they occur only inside an argument in the countable-product-measures annex, lines 31-35).

Durrett's measurable-map, random-variable and random-vector definitions (pp. 10, 15) are covered. Not supplied: the source's notation 'X in F' for F-measurability ('we will say that X is F-measurable or write X in F', p. 10), which the source uses throughout (for example for conditional expectations); no on-route item records it.

components.note: Durrett Thm 1.3.1, the sigma-field generated by X (1.3.1) and Exercise 1.3.1 (pp. 15, 17); discrete spaces make every function measurable (p. 10, lines 263-265).
Handbook example; the four-set sigma(Y) and the non-measurability of X verified.

components.gap: Indicator and simple-function definitions are covered (Durrett p. 10; Exercise 1.3.7). Not supplied: the terminology warning attached to the source's indicator definition (p. 10), that analysts call 1_A the characteristic function of A whereas in probability that term means something quite different (Section 3.3); no on-route item gives it.

components.note: Durrett Thms 1.3.4-1.3.6 (pp. 15-16): composition, vectors (hence Borel functions of several variables), sums and continuous functions.

components.gap: Durrett (p. 17) defines a random variable as a function whose domain is a set D in F and whose range is R* = [-infinity, infinity], measurable for the Borel sets of R* in the topology generated by [-infinity,a), (a,b), (b,infinity]; he defines 'X_n converges almost surely' as P(Omega_o) = 1 for Omega_o = {lim X_n exists}, with no prescribed limit, and adopts X_infinity = limsup X_n. The definition admits only maps defined on all of Omega (line 237), uses the sigma-algebra generated by [-infinity,a] without relating it to the order-topology Borel sets, and defines a.s. convergence only to a specified real X (lines 317-319). The domain-D variant, the order-topology description and the X_infinity convention are not supplied on the input route; the limit-free notion appears only for series of independent terms in a later, unreferenced chapter (independent-random-series.tex lines 23-31).

Durrett Thm 1.3.7 (p. 16) and the simple approximation are covered. Not supplied: the source's measurability of the convergence set Omega_o = {w: lim X_n exists} = {limsup X_n - liminf X_n = 0} (pp. 16-17); the theorem proves only that {X_n -> X} is measurable for a given real X. A related statement appears only later and unreferenced, for partial sums (limsup-events-and-zero-one-laws.tex lines 159-161: convergence of S_n to a finite value or to plus or minus infinity is a tail event).

Durrett's distribution mu(A) = P(X in A) (p. 10) is covered as the pushforward. Not supplied: the source's notation mu = P o X^{-1} (Figure 1.3, p. 10) and its terminology 'equal in distribution' with the notation X =d Y for random variables inducing the same distribution (pp. 11-12); the definition speaks only of the 'same law', and no on-route item records the source terms.

components.note: Durrett p. 10 (the distribution is a probability measure), with image laws and atomic sums.
Durrett App. A.1 p. 456: pi-system and lambda-system definitions.

components.gap: The pi-lambda theorem (Durrett Thm A.1.4, pp. 456-457) is covered. Durrett's Thm A.1.5 (p. 457) states that measures nu1, nu2 (on sigma-fields F1, F2) agreeing on a pi-system P that contains A_n increasing to Omega with nu_i(A_n) finite agree on sigma(P); the theorem here states only two probability measures on sigma(C), and the sigma-finite version with an exhausting sequence from the pi-system is not on the input route (the measure-extension uniqueness proof treats only agreement on an algebra). Exercise A.1.1 (p. 458; two probability measures on {1,2,3,4} agreeing on a generating class that is not a pi-system) is also not rendered.

Durrett Thm 1.2.1 (i)-(v) (pp. 10-11), Exercise 1.2.3 (countably many discontinuities, p. 14) and equality of laws iff equal distribution functions (pp. 11-12).
source_locators: Durrett Thm 1.2.1 pp. 10-11; pp. 11-12; Exercise 1.2.3 p. 14

components.gap: The discrete-law definition (Durrett p. 13) is covered. Not supplied: the source's companion Example 1.2.9 (p. 14), F(x) = sum_i alpha_i 1_[q_i, infinity)(x) for an enumeration of the rationals with alpha_i > 0 summing to one, showing that the distribution function of a discrete law 'can be quite wild' (it jumps at every rational); on the route it is only mentioned in passing (probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02b-p15-002.tex lines 292-293) without construction or proof.

The boundary's pointers resolve (Thm 1.2.2, Thms 1.1.4/1.1.9, App. A.1 to the measure-extension chapter; secs 1.4-1.6; densities and the Cantor law; conditional expectation). It does not account for Durrett's measures on R^d in sec. 1.1 (pp. 6-9): the conditions (i)-(iv) on F: R^d -> [0,1], including nonnegativity of the signed rectangle increment over the vertices, the two-dimensional counterexample (Figure 1.1) that satisfies (i)-(iii) yet would give mass -1/3 at (1,1), and Theorem 1.1.11 (a unique probability measure with mu(A) equal to that increment for every finite rectangle). These are not on the input route (only the uninserted w02c-p15-002 file renders Theorem 1.1.11); only product-form instances appear elsewhere (product Stieltjes laws in independent-random-variables.tex lines 185-195, Lebesgue measure on R^d as a product in convolution-gamma-normal.tex), and the measure-extension boundary (lines 365-367 there) leaves multidimensional Stieltjes constructions as 'separate results' without a location. The boundary also does not refer to the Gaussian tail bounds of Thm 1.2.6, present on the route only from Feller (de-moivre-laplace-and-stirling.tex lines 71-95), or to the sections' exercises.
